subject: biology
title: Pathogen Patrol
welcome_lead: Today you'll meet the four families of pathogen and learn how your immune system fights back.
meta_desc: GCSE Biology Infection & Response foundations — bacteria, viruses, fungi, protists and your immune defences.
final_note: You can now name all four pathogen groups, give an example of each, and explain how phagocytes and lymphocytes protect you.

concepts.def: Living cells that release toxins (e.g. Salmonella)
Tiny particle that hijacks host cells (e.g. measles)
Protein from lymphocytes that locks onto antigens

walkthroughs.body_html:
A pathogen is a microorganism that causes disease. There are four families you need to know.

Bacteria — living cells that release toxins. Example: Salmonella (food poisoning).

Viruses — tiny particles that take over your cells. Examples: measles, HIV, TMV (tobacco mosaic virus in plants).

Fungi — spore-makers. Example: rose black spot on plants.

Protists — single-celled eukaryotes. Example: the malaria parasite, spread by mosquitoes.

Pathogens travel in three main ways:

Air — droplets from coughs and sneezes (e.g. measles).

Water — drinking dirty water (e.g. cholera bacteria).

Direct contact — touch or body fluids (e.g. HIV, athlete's foot).

Hygiene, isolation and vaccination all cut these transmission routes.

If a pathogen gets in, your white blood cells spring into action.

Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens — like Pac-Man.

Lymphocytes make antibodies that lock onto markers called antigens on the pathogen.

Lymphocytes also release antitoxins to neutralise bacterial toxins. After the fight, memory cells remember the pathogen for next time.

mcqs.q: What do lymphocytes produce to lock onto pathogens?
options: Antigens
Antibodies
Antibiotics
Platelets

mcqs.q: What is the key structural difference between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
options: Each gene codes for an organ or body part as a whole.
Prokaryotes are always smaller than 1 micrometre and have no cytoplasm.
Eukaryotes have a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; prokaryotes do not.
Prokaryotes have no DNA — that's why they have no nucleus.

mcqs.q: What does a gene code for?
options: Typically a polypeptide (protein) — through transcription to mRNA and translation by ribosomes.
A gene codes for a specific physical feature like eye colour directly.
Vaccines provide antibodies for life by adding them directly to the blood.
Each gene codes for an organ or body part as a whole.

mcqs.q: How do vaccines protect you from a disease?
options: Vaccines provide antibodies for life by adding them directly to the blood.
Each gene codes for an organ or body part as a whole.
They expose your immune system to a harmless form of the pathogen so memory cells form, allowing rapid response if exposed later.
Vaccines kill the pathogen if it ever enters the body.

mcqs.q: A patient has 5 different white blood cells working: 2 phagocytes and 3 lymphocytes. If each lymphocyte makes 4 antibodies per minute, how many antibodies are made in 1 minute?
A graph shows antibody levels after a first and second exposure to the same pathogen. The second response is faster and larger. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Memory cells from the first exposure cause a faster second response.
The pathogen became stronger the second time.
Antibodies are made only on the first exposure.
The second response is slower because of immunity.

mcqs.q: A patient has a bacterial infection and a viral infection. The doctor prescribes antibiotics. These will help with:
options: The bacterial infection only
The viral infection only
Both infections equally
Neither infection

mcqs.q: White blood cells defend the body in different ways. Which describes the role of a phagocyte?
options: It engulfs and digests pathogens.
It produces antibodies specific to one antigen.
It carries oxygen to the infection.
It clots the blood at a wound.

mcqs.q: A vaccine is given to a population to reduce the spread of a disease. When enough people are immune, even the unvaccinated are partly protected. This is called:
options: Herd immunity
Active infection
Antibiotic resistance
A placebo effect

sequence.def: Microbe with foreign antigens breaches the body
Phagocyte engulfs and digests the pathogen
